query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, phase stability and the retention of strong high-temperature strength, corrosion/radiation resistance, and cryogenic toughness are governed by the controlled formation of a nanoscale, coherent B2 (ordered) phase embedded in a disordered matrix. This dual‐phase microstructure arises from a balance between the high configurational entropy (which favors single-phase solid solution) and local chemical ordering tendencies (driven by negative mixing enthalpies among select pairs such as Al with Cr/Co), leading to finely dispersed, coherent precipitates that act as dispersion strengtheners, defect sinks, and barriers to coarsening.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast or conventionally processed Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA that is either single-phase or contains only incipient, nonoptimized ordering.
generation.intervention: A controlled heat-treatment (or aging process) designed to promote the nucleation and stable dispersion of nanoscale, coherent B2 precipitates within the disordered matrix.
generation.conditions: The treatment and subsequent tests are performed over a range of temperatures—from cryogenic (to assess toughness) through intermediate (mechanical and irradiation testing) to high temperatures (for strength and oxidation/corrosion performance). A controlled comparison is made between samples subjected to the heat-treatment versus a baseline sample (as-cast or with overcoarsened/incoherent precipitates).
generation.structural_mediator: A network of coherent nanoscale B2 (ordered) precipitates enriched in elements like Al and Cr, which are distributed throughout a disordered matrix.
generation.mechanism: The precipitates form by local short-range ordering that counteracts the full effect of high entropy, with atomic interactions (e.g., between Al and Cr/Co) driving a limited, coherent ordering. These nanoscale precipitates serve several functions: they impede dislocation motion (enhancing high-temperature strength), provide interfaces that serve as efficient defect sinks (improving radiation tolerance), and stabilize protective oxide-forming element distributions (enhancing environmental resistance), while the fine size and coherence help retain toughness at cryogenic temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline single-phase or non-optimally precipitated alloy, the heat-treated alloy with a controlled distribution of coherent B2 precipitates will exhibit higher tensile and creep strength at elevated temperatures, lower oxidation and corrosion rates, improved defect absorption under irradiation, and maintained or enhanced cryogenic toughness.
generation.baseline: Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs produced without this tailored heat-treatment, which either remain entirely as a single disordered phase or develop coarse/incoherent precipitates that do not contribute beneficially.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold within a compositional window (near equiatomic ratios) where the competing effects of high mixing entropy and local ordering are balanced. It applies to heat treatments within a specific temperature–time profile that promotes nanoscale coherence. Extreme deviations in composition or processing that lead to either excessive phase separation or complete suppression of ordering are outside its validity.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative contributions of each elemental pairing to the ordering tendency and the long-term thermal cyclic stability of the dual-phase microstructure remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA samples: one set undergoes the tailored heat-treatment to promote coherent nanoscale B2 precipitate formation, while a control set is either left in the as-cast state or purposely overaged to induce incoherent or overly coarse precipitates. Expose both sample sets to mechanical testing (tensile and creep) at high and cryogenic temperatures, oxidation/corrosion testing in relevant environments, and simulated radiation damage tests.
measurements: Microstructural characterization (TEM, XRD) to determine precipitate size, coherence, and distribution
Mechanical tests to assess tensile strength, ductility, and creep resistance at high temperatures and toughness at cryogenic temperatures
Oxidation and corrosion rate measurements in reactive environments
Radiation damage assessments (e.g., ion irradiation) with subsequent defect characterization
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with controlled coherent B2 precipitates do not exhibit statistically significant improvements—i.e., if mechanical strength, oxidation/corrosion resistance, and radiation tolerance are not enhanced relative to the baseline (or if similar performance is obtained without the presence of coherent precipitates)—then the mechanistic role of the nanoscale, coherent B2 phase in governing phase stability and properties is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. While the AlCoFeNi high entropy alloy exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature, both the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, and lower annealing temperatures lead to a tendency for this system to decompose into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC solid solution. The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature, as demonstrated in this investigation by comparing and contrasting AlCoFeNi with the AlCo 0.5 Cr 0.5 FeNi alloy. The resulting phase stability has been rationalized based on solution thermodynamic predictions. Additionally, it is shown that replacement of Co by Cr in the AlCoFeNi alloy resulted in a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization and increase in coercivity. The microhardness is also strongly influenced by the composition and the length scale of B2 + BCC decomposition in these high entropy alloys.

Abstract High entropy or compositionally complex alloys provide opportunities for optimization towards new high-temperature materials. Improvements in the equiatomic alloy Al 17 Co 17 Cr 17 Cu 17 Fe 17 Ni 17 (at.%) led to the base alloy for this work with the chemical composition Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (at.%). Characterization of the beneficial particle-strengthened microstructure by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and observation of good mechanical properties at elevated temperatures arose the need of accomplishing further optimization steps. For this purpose, the refractory metals hafnium and molybdenum were added in small amounts (0.5 and 1.0 at.% respectively) because of their well-known positive effects on mechanical properties of Ni-based superalloys. By correlation of microstructural examinations using SEM with tensile tests in the temperature range of room temperature up to 900 °C, conclusions could be drawn for further optimization steps. Keywords: HEA, high entropy alloys, compositionally complex alloys, mechanical characterization
